beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson five. Buffers, and how strong an acid is. Last time, pH was minus the log of the H plus concentration. [[cell]]A living cell works best close to pH seven, [[blood]]and human blood is held near seven point four. [[swing]]A swing of even one unit changes the H plus concentration tenfold, and proteins can stop working. [[ask]]So how does a cell stay steady when acids and bases keep arriving?
beats.buffer: The answer is a buffer. [[water]]Take a beaker of pure water at pH seven, and add a little acid, one thousandth of a mole per liter of H plus. [[drop]]The pH falls to three. Four units, from one drop. [[buf]]Now try a beaker of acetic acid and acetate, at pH four point seven six. [[add]]Add the same acid, and the pH slips to four point seven five. [[def]]A buffer is a solution that resists change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
beats.comp: Why does it work? [[pair]]A buffer holds two partners: a weak acid, and its conjugate base, the particle left when the acid has given up a proton. [[acetic]]Acetic acid is the weak acid, and acetate is its conjugate base. [[hin]]When H plus arrives, acetate takes it up and becomes acetic acid. [[hout]]When hydroxide arrives, acetic acid gives up H plus, which joins the hydroxide to make water. [[both]]Either way, one partner is spent and the other is made, so the H plus concentration barely moves. [[base]]The same works the other way round: a weak base, like ammonia, with its conjugate acid, ammonium.
beats.blood: Your blood uses this. [[pair]]Carbonic acid is a weak acid, and bicarbonate is its conjugate base. [[hin]]Acid from working muscles meets bicarbonate, which takes up the H plus. [[hout]]Extra base meets carbonic acid, which gives H plus back. [[hold]]That is one reason blood stays close to seven point four.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which partner takes up added H plus?
beats.ka: Now, how strong is the weak acid? [[split]]Put a thousand acetic acid molecules in water, and only about thirteen give up a proton. Most stay whole. [[strong]]A strong acid, hydrochloric acid, splits essentially all of them. [[ka]]The dissociation constant, Ka, measures this. It compares the products, H plus and the conjugate base, with the acid left whole. For acetic acid, Ka is about one point seven times ten to the minus five. [[pka]]Chemists turn it into a pKa, minus the log of Ka, so acetic acid has a pKa of four point seven six, about four point eight. [[dir]]Watch the direction. A smaller Ka means less dissociation, a larger pKa, and a weaker acid. [[none]]For a strong acid the acid is almost gone, so a pKa tells us little. It is only useful for weak acids.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which acid is weaker?
beats.proto: Acids also differ in how many protons they can give. [[mono]]Acetic acid has just one, so it is monoprotic. [[poly]]Phosphoric acid has three, so it is polyprotic, and it has one pKa for each proton, about two point two, seven point two, and twelve point three. [[cellp]]The middle one, near seven, suits the cell.
beats.range: So where does a buffer work? [[axis]]Here is the pH axis, with acetic acid's pKa at four point eight. [[mid]]At pH equal to pKa, half the acid is whole and half is acetate. Both partners are plentiful, so capacity is greatest. [[low]]One unit lower, at pH three point eight, about nine percent is acetate, and the buffer is running short of base. [[high]]One unit higher, at five point eight, about ninety-one percent is acetate, and it is running short of acid. [[rng]]So a buffer works within pKa plus or minus one, here three point eight to five point eight, and best at pH four point eight. [[out]]Outside that, one partner is nearly used up, and the pH moves freely.
beats.rain: Last, acid in the sky. [[clean]]Rain is slightly acid even when the air is clean, because carbon dioxide dissolves in it, and its pH sits near five point six. [[def]]Acid precipitation, rain, snow or fog below pH five point six, forms mainly when pollutants, such as sulfur and nitrogen oxides from burning fuel, mix with water in the air. [[lake]]In lakes and streams, the acid harms the life in them. [[soil]]In soils, it changes the chemistry, and it contributes to the decline of some forests.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Cells need a steady pH near seven, and a buffer, a weak acid with its conjugate base, absorbs added H plus or hydroxide. [[w2]]Ka measures how far a weak acid dissociates, and pKa is minus the log of Ka. Smaller Ka, larger pKa, weaker acid. [[w3]]A buffer works within pKa plus or minus one, and best at pH equal to pKa. [[w4]]Acid precipitation is rain, snow or fog below pH five point six. [[end]]Now try the practice.
